rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Modern human power, including electricity and atomic technology, has grown, but ships still drown and machinery fails at sea.
rows.anchor: even today every now and then we read about various sea ships drowning in the sea like tablets of aspirin dissolving in water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable's signs are lessons for the patient and grateful, who reflect on life's events and meet adversity with hope and trust in God, whose acts are never without wisdom.
rows.anchor: those who are patient and grateful will find many a lesson in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In favorable circumstances people should thank God for what they receive, since God can also take it away; the unaware become arrogant with favor or frustrated in hardship and miss faith's sweetness.
rows.anchor: just as God has the power to give, He also has the power to take away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about God's will is coordinated with the ships remaining still, while the intervening clause is parenthetical and states the parable's purpose.
rows.anchor: is a parenthetical one and is meant to point to the objective of this parable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the parenthesis, the passage says God may stop the wind and ships, drown passengers for their deeds, or pardon many and bring them safely ashore.
rows.anchor: He has the power to exercise any of these three options

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Success should not make anyone proud: the successful should be grateful, while a person in calamity should be patient and hope for good from God.
rows.anchor: it is not right for any person in this world to become proud of his success

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative word has an omitted coordinated clause, a grammatical ellipsis of the kind also found in earlier and later sūrahs; 45:22 is an example.
rows.anchor: its co-ordinated sentence must be regarded as suppressed. Several examples of such suppression can be seen in the previous sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ellipsis supplies a purpose: God takes revenge on those who split hairs over His revelations and shows that they have nowhere to escape.
rows.anchor: so that those who do hair-splitting regarding the revelations of God become aware of the reality that they have no place to run from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yūnus 10:22–23 gives a parallel: people face a violent storm at sea, vow gratitude if rescued, then rebel after God delivers them.
rows.anchor: Here is an example from Sūrah Yūnus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly wealth and favors are fleeting provisions; what God has in the Hereafter is better and enduring for believers who trust Him, so they should desire that future.
rows.anchor: whatever lies in the Hereafter with God is better then these provisions and also eternal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trust in God is the true provision for the journey toward the eternal Hereafter; reaching it requires relying on God and leaving whatever obstructs His path.
rows.anchor: for those people who are desirous of the eternal kingdom of the Hereafter, the real provision for their journey is trust in God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verses list further traits of those worthy of the reward described earlier.
rows.anchor: some more traits of the people, who are worthy of the aforementioned reward, are mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These traits identify the Muslims oppressed by the arrogant Quraysh and driven from their homes as worthy of that reward.
rows.anchor: those Muslims who had become the target of all kinds of oppression from the arrogant Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revealed near the migration to Madīnah, the passage signals victory and a coming change from a scattered group to a political community able to defend itself with God's permission.
rows.anchor: now the Almighty is creating a situation in which they will be politically organized as a community

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance describes how believers will naturally act through faith and trust when circumstances change; it is not framed as a direct command.
rows.anchor: this guidance is not in the garb of a directive; it is stated as an obvious consequence of faith and trust in God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that angels are God's daughters is refuted because its proponents dislike daughters for themselves, making the claim foolish and disrespectful to God.
rows.anchor: people regard the angels to be the daughters of God even though they dislike having daughters for themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Appealing to forefathers does not establish idolatry; the idolaters need evidence from revelation, reason, or human nature, or they face the fate of earlier deniers.
rows.anchor: The only argument they have to associate the angels in Godhead is that their forefathers regarded this to be so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham, who renounced his people's idolatry and settled Ishmael in Mecca, is Quraysh's true ancestor; the inherited tradition is migration from polytheism, not idolatry.
rows.anchor: Their real ancestor is Abraham (sws) who left their nation by uttering these historic words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rejecters' rebellion stems from affluence, which cannot outweigh the Hereafter; Satan's blindfold will lift too late, so the Prophet must persist in preaching the true religion attested by all prophets.
rows.anchor: The real thing which has become a source of trial for them is their affluence even though this affluence cannot tilt the scales of God’s balance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is directed to hold firmly to his preaching because the religion he calls to is the true religion, confirmed by all God's prophets.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is then directed to hold fast to his preaching efforts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Jesus both called people to monotheism; Pharaoh and his chiefs rejected Moses' successive signs for the same arrogant reason as Quraysh and met their deserved fate, which Quraysh will also face.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) showed great signs one after the other to the Pharaoh and his chiefs

rows.speaker: Quraysh
rows.claim: Some Quraysh opponents contend that their own deities are better than Jesus and think the Qur’an invokes him so people will treat him as God's son, as Christians do.
rows.anchor: the pugnacious among the Quraysh are propelled to argue with the Prophet (sws). They contend that their own deities are better than Jesus (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an presents Jesus as a preacher of tawḥīd: he taught that God alone is Lord of both him and his audience and must alone be served; later generations altered his call.
rows.anchor: God alone is my Lord and He alone is your Lord too; so serve Him only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage first depicts the fate of those who accept the true call and then the fate of those who deny it.
rows.anchor: the fate of those people is mentioned who will profess faith in this true call; then the fate of those people is depicted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should ignore the stubborn; they will witness their fate and learn the truth about the angels' intercession on which they relied arrogantly.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is assured that he should ignore these stubborn people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every part of Sūrah al-Zukhruf relates deeply to its central theme, and the whole sūrah forms a harmonious unit from beginning to end.
rows.anchor: each part of it is deeply related to its central theme

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People can innately distinguish guidance from misguidance when their conscience is alive and they are not stubborn, arrogant, or obdurate.
rows.anchor: the ability to distinguish between guidance and misguidance has been innately endowed by the Almighty in man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When nations stubbornly and arrogantly refuse to heed messengers, God takes them to account for this ingratitude; readers should observe the fate of rejecters.
rows.anchor: when the stubbornness and arrogance of nations reached the limit that they refused to listen and accept the calls of the messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's migration and renunciation of polytheism refute Quraysh's claim to have inherited idolatry: Abraham is their real ancestor, and his example remains in both branches of his progeny.
rows.anchor: their real ancestor is Abraham (sws) who left his people because of polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the historical example, the passage highlights Quraysh's real rebelliousness and assures the Prophet to persist: he calls to the messengers' true path, while God may judge opponents but grants them respite by His established practice.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is assured that he should adhere to his preaching
